sections.Run Context: Target: examples/RagChatbot_MCPServer. Authoritative inputs: smith/tool_definitions.json (10 tools, source http://localhost:8000/sse, transport sse), smith/system_vars.json (roles: employee/manager per guidance.txt, but action_description/roles/teams object -- note: system_vars.json declares roles ["employee","manager"] while runtime code (opa_config.py/opa_client.py) uses ["user","manager"] as the actual role vocabulary), guidance.txt (19 rules). Source files inspected: mcp_server.py (tool registrations/implementations), opa_client.py (OPAClient/UniversalOPAClient, user-context store), opa_config.py (role table, session init), run_llm_with_mcp.py (Streamlit client/agent, LLMGuard calls, tool dispatch), create_ticket.py, rag_pipeline.py, rag_salary.py (raw_* implementations), llm_guard_config.py (EnhancedLLMGuardWrapper scanners), data_sources/hr_database.py (HRDatabase/CompensationDatabase/PurchaseDatabase fixtures). Followed at most 2 hops from each registered tool (mcp_server.py -> create_ticket.py/rag_pipeline.py/rag_salary.py/opa_client.py/data_sources.hr_database); did not expand into langchain/openai/mcp/llm_guard library internals.
sections.Trust Boundaries: Boundary 1: Streamlit UI (run_llm_with_mcp.py) selects user_role via a client-side selectbox with no authentication; this role is pushed to the MCP server only by calling a tool named set_user_role, which does not exist in mcp_server.py or tool_definitions.json (unresolved/dynamic -- Unknown, not proven absent). Boundary 2: MCP client (run_llm_with_mcp.py) to MCP server (mcp_server.py) over SSE at http://localhost:8000/sse; tool arguments arrive as LLM-generated JSON, parsed with json.loads and passed through uninspected. Boundary 3: MCP server tool implementations to in-process fixture data sources (data_sources/hr_database.py) -- no network hop, no additional authorization check observed inside tool bodies. Boundary 4: MCP server to external OPA server (opa_client.OPAClient posts to http://localhost:8181) -- present as library/HTTP-client code in opa_client.py, but no call site in mcp_server.py's tool bodies invokes evaluate_policy, so this boundary is defined but not wired into the request path for any tool visible in this tree.
sections.Data Flow: Request: Streamlit user input -> enforce_input() LLMGuard prompt-injection/PII scan (with a business-safe-word allowlist and malicious-substring blocklist) -> chat() appends system+user messages (system message embeds the client-asserted user_profile dict verbatim) -> OpenAI-compatible LLM selects a tool + JSON arguments -> ConnectionManager.call_tool over MCP SSE -> mcp_server.py tool function executes business logic directly against data_sources/hr_database.py in-memory fixtures (no pre-execution policy check observed) -> raw tool return string. Response: tool return string -> enforce_output() LLMGuard output scan (PII redaction, banned literal substrings, toxicity/relevance) -> appended as a 'tool' message -> further LLM turns until a final assistant message -> enforce_output() again -> rendered to Streamlit UI. Role sync path: role selection in the sidebar -> initialize_user_session()/set_user_context() (local in-process dict update in opa_client.py) and a best-effort call_tool('set_user_role', ...) against the MCP server, which is not a tool defined in mcp_server.py.

Layers.Role: Renders chat UI, holds client-selected user_role in st.session_state, assembles system/user messages, drives the tool-calling loop against an OpenAI-compatible chat model, dispatches MCP tool calls, applies LLMGuard input/output scanning.
Layers.Inputs: Chat text input; sidebar role selectbox (user|manager); st.session_state.user_profile; MCP tool list/schemas fetched at startup.
Layers.Outputs: Sanitized assistant response rendered to chat UI; outbound MCP tool_call requests with LLM-generated JSON arguments; a best-effort set_user_role tool call.
Layers.Current enforcement: LLMGuard prompt-injection/PII/toxicity scan on input (enforce_input) with a hardcoded business-safe-word allowlist that can override a flagged scan; LLMGuard output scan (enforce_output) except messages starting with the deny marker are passed through unfiltered.

Layers.Role: FastMCP server exposing 10 @mcp.tool()-decorated functions over SSE (source http://localhost:8000/sse per tool_definitions.json).
Layers.Inputs: MCP tool_call requests (tool name + JSON arguments) from the client over SSE.
Layers.Outputs: String tool results (plain text, JSON-encoded text, or CSV-formatted text) returned over MCP.
Layers.Current enforcement: None observed at registration/dispatch level; no decorator or pre-call check wraps any @mcp.tool() function in this file (a commented-out @policy_check(...) decorator exists for two now-disabled tools, and policy_check is not defined anywhere in the inspected tree).

Layers.Role: Business logic for each tool: ticketing (create_ticket.py), RAG Q&A over PDFs (rag_pipeline.py for work policy, rag_salary.py for salary PDF), and inline logic in mcp_server.py for send_email, export_content_as_file, get_w2_form, return_product, view_team_compensation, export_compensation_data, email_compensation_report, purchase.
Layers.Inputs: Tool arguments as declared in tool_definitions.json; in-process user context (opa_client.get_current_user_context()) for the two compensation tools and purchase.
Layers.Outputs: Formatted strings/JSON/CSV containing business data, including sensitive HR fields for the compensation tools.
Layers.Current enforcement: None: view_team_compensation and export_compensation_data include sensitive fields (ssn, personal_email, home_address, bank_account, emergency_contact, healthcare_plan/id) unconditionally whenever the underlying fixture record has them, with only a code comment stating 'policy enforcement will filter based on permissions'; no such filtering call exists in the function body. email_compensation_report and send_email perform no domain allowlist/blocklist check despite guidance rules 6-8, 18-19 requiring one.

Layers.Role: Defines an in-process user-context store (current_user_context dict, set via set_user_context), a role->permission table (USER_ROLES: user, manager), an OPAClient that POSTs to an OPA server's allow/deny endpoints, a UniversalOPAClient that can transform tool calls into a universal Rego-shaped input (kind/action/name/arguments/extensions.subject/...), and a hardcoded _fail_secure_decision fallback used only when the OPA server is unreachable.
Layers.Inputs: user_id/user_role/kwargs passed to set_user_context; tool name + arguments passed to build_universal_input/transform_to_universal_schema; OPA server responses over HTTP.
Layers.Outputs: current_user_context dict read by mcp_server.py tool bodies; a universal-schema dict shaped for OPA input.extensions.subject.*; an allow/deny boolean plus reason (when actually invoked).
Layers.Current enforcement: This layer is fully built (schema shaping, fail-secure heuristics for role/domain/external-sharing/time-range/sensitive-fields) but is never called from any @mcp.tool() function body in mcp_server.py in this tree -- it is present machinery, not a wired enforcement point. It is the intended future OPA interception layer.

Layers.File: llm_guard_config.py (imported in run_llm_with_mcp.py as RagChatbot_MCPServer.llm_guard_copy, a module not found in this tree)
Layers.Role: LLMGuard-based scanners: input side blocks/redacts prompt injection, invisible text, PII (via Anonymize), banned substrings (including literal words like 'ssn', 'bypass', 'ignore all'), secrets, toxicity, non-English text; output side redacts PII/sensitive entities, banned literal substrings (example SSNs/addresses/bank accounts from the fixture data), toxicity, and checks relevance/no-refusal.
Layers.Inputs: Raw user/system chat text (input side); tool_call_id result strings and the user prompt (output side).
Layers.Outputs: Sanitized/redacted text plus an is_valid boolean.
Layers.Current enforcement: Prompt-layer guardrail only; operates on free text, not on structured tool arguments or subject identity, and is bypassed for provider-formatted deny messages (text.startswith('🚫')). The import path used by run_llm_with_mcp.py (llm_guard_copy) does not match the only guard module present (llm_guard_config.py); this is recorded as an unresolved path rather than assumed broken.

Layers.Role: In-memory fixture classes HRDatabase (employees, managers), CompensationDatabase (compensation_data, sensitive_data), and a purchase catalog/rules database referenced as purchase_db in mcp_server.py.
Layers.Inputs: None (static Python dict literals initialized at import time).
Layers.Outputs: Employee, compensation, and sensitive-field records keyed by employee/manager id; vendor catalog and purchase-category rules.
Layers.Current enforcement: None; all records are returned to whichever tool queries them, with field-level access left entirely to the (unimplemented) 'policy enforcement' referenced only in comments.

Prompt Inputs.Source: Streamlit st.chat_input(), i.e. direct end-user text.
Prompt Inputs.Consumer: enforce_input() LLMGuard scan, then embedded into the 'user' role message sent to the LLM as 'Current task/question: ' + question.
Prompt Inputs.Trust / influence: Untrusted; scanned for prompt injection/PII/toxicity, but a hardcoded business-safe-word allowlist can override a scanner block, and if no malicious-pattern match is found the text is still allowed through with only a warning even when LLMGuard itself flagged it.

Prompt Inputs.Source: Client-side session state set from the sidebar role selectbox; not authenticated.
Prompt Inputs.Consumer: Interpolated verbatim into the system prompt ('The current user's profile: ' + str(...)) sent to the LLM.
Prompt Inputs.Trust / influence: Self-asserted client data placed directly in the system prompt; the LLM (not a structured pre-execution check) is the only consumer that 'sees' the role for reasoning about what the user is allowed to do, since no tool body reads this profile.

Prompt Inputs.Field or data: memory_text (prior turns, up to last 10 messages)
Prompt Inputs.Source: st.session_state.messages, built from prior user/assistant turns in the same Streamlit session.
Prompt Inputs.Consumer: Appended into the system prompt as conversation history for the LLM.
Prompt Inputs.Trust / influence: Mixed trust: includes prior user input (untrusted) and prior assistant/tool output (which may include real HR data if a compensation tool was called earlier in the session), re-fed into later prompts without re-scanning through enforce_input.

Prompt Inputs.Field or data: retrieved PDF context (work_rules_and_regulations_2016.pdf via rag_pipeline.py; salary_summary.pdf via rag_salary.py)
Prompt Inputs.Source: Local PDF files loaded and chunked at first use via PDFPlumberLoader + InMemoryVectorStore similarity search.
Prompt Inputs.Consumer: Interpolated into the RAG prompt template's {context} slot and sent to the underlying chat LLM (ChatOpenAI) for ask_for_workpolicy; rag_salary.py's raw_ask_for_salary exists but is not wired to any @mcp.tool() in mcp_server.py (ask_for_salary tool is commented out).
Prompt Inputs.Trust / influence: Treated as trusted reference content by the RAG prompt, but is not passed through enforce_output before being embedded in a further LLM call inside ask_for_workpolicy itself; the final answer is scanned by enforce_output only when the *tool's overall return string* reaches the outer chat() loop.

Prompt Inputs.Field or data: tool output text (e.g. compensation JSON/CSV, email confirmations)
Prompt Inputs.Consumer: Appended as a 'role: tool' message back into the LLM conversation for the next turn, after enforce_output(); also directly surfaced to the user once the LLM stops calling tools.
Prompt Inputs.Trust / influence: Treated as at least partly trusted (fed back into the LLM as ground truth); enforce_output applies PII/substring redaction, but denial messages beginning with the specific emoji marker bypass all output scanning.

Enforcement Points.Current: enforce_input(): LLMGuard PromptInjection/Anonymize/BanSubstrings/Secrets/Toxicity/Language scan, with a business-safe-word allowlist that can override a scanner block and a narrow hardcoded malicious-substring list that is the only thing that actually raises a blocking exception.
Enforcement Points.Available (OPA-interceptable): Not directly OPA-interceptable as implemented (free-text heuristics, not structured input.args/subject fields); an OPA decision could still gate whether a request reaches the LLM at all if the client called out to OPA before invoking the model, but no such call exists today.
Enforcement Points.Blind spots: The business-safe-word allowlist can let a flagged prompt-injection attempt through if it also contains an allowlisted business word; conversation memory (memory_text) is re-injected into later prompts without being re-scanned.

Enforcement Points.Current: None: no decorator, middleware, or explicit call to opa_client.evaluate_policy wraps any active @mcp.tool() function.
Enforcement Points.Available (OPA-interceptable): Yes -- this is the natural pre-execution point: input.args.* for every tool (department, select_fields, external_sharing, destination, amount, format, export_type, etc.) is fully declared in tool_definitions.json and available at the moment each tool function is entered, so a Rego decision keyed on tool name + declared arguments could gate every tool call before business logic runs.
Enforcement Points.Blind spots: None structural at this layer for argument-based checks; the blind spot is that role/identity (input.extensions.subject.*) is not reliably available here (see Runtime Subject Context) because it is self-asserted and not verified, so any future policy gating tool arguments would still need a trustworthy subject source to enforce role-based rules like guidance rules 1-2, 4-5, 9-10.

Enforcement Points.Current: In-process mutable dict updated by whichever caller invokes set_user_context; no authentication step observed anywhere in the inspected tree.
Enforcement Points.Available (OPA-interceptable): The shape needed (extensions.subject.id/roles/teams/permissions) is already defined in UniversalOPAClient.get_principal_context()/build_universal_input(), so once wired, role-based decisions are OPA-expressible; the field values would be exactly as trustworthy as their current provenance, which is client-self-asserted with no verification mechanism documented anywhere in this tree.
Enforcement Points.Blind spots: True blind spot: there is no identity/authentication layer in this codebase. Any OPA policy keyed on input.extensions.subject.roles would be enforcing a client-asserted claim, not a verified one, unless an integrity mechanism is added upstream (out of scope for this guidance-only phase to invent).

Enforcement Points.Current: Fully implemented client (OPAClient.evaluate_policy, UniversalOPAClient) with a documented fail-secure fallback (_fail_secure_decision) for role/domain/external-sharing/time-range/sensitive-field checks, but zero call sites from any active tool in mcp_server.py.
Enforcement Points.Available (OPA-interceptable): Yes in principle -- this is precisely the pre-execution OPA hook the rest of the system was designed around; it is simply unconnected to the live tool-call path in this snapshot of the code.
Enforcement Points.Blind spots: None structural; the gap is wiring, not expressibility. Recorded as a gap for downstream phases, not invented as an enforcement point that exists today.

Enforcement Points.Current: enforce_output(): LLMGuard Sensitive/BanSubstrings(example literals)/Toxicity/Relevance/NoRefusal scan on every tool result and final assistant message, except messages starting with the deny-emoji marker, which bypass scanning entirely.
Enforcement Points.Available (OPA-interceptable): Not OPA-interceptable as a pre-execution decision (it runs after the tool already executed and returned real data); it is a post-hoc mitigation, not a substitute for pre-execution argument/subject-based gating.
Enforcement Points.Blind spots: By the time this runs, view_team_compensation/export_compensation_data have already assembled and returned full sensitive records into the tool-result string; BanSubstrings only catches the specific example literal values hardcoded in llm_guard_config.py (e.g. two example SSNs/addresses/bank-account suffixes), not the full range of fixture records in data_sources/hr_database.py, so most real sensitive values in this dataset would not be redacted by the literal-substring list.

Undeclared Fields.Consequence: Guidance rule 1 ('Managers: View only the requested manager's team compensation data ... via view_team_compensation') cannot be expressed as an OPA predicate today, because there is no declared, trustworthy field identifying which manager/team is making the request or which department was actually queried -- the declared department argument is ignored by the implementation (see Tool Arguments).

Undeclared Fields.Declared by: The destination argument is declared by email_compensation_report and recipient_email by send_email; the domain values/lists themselves (ibm.com allow, the five blocked domains) are guidance-only literals not declared in tool_definitions.json or system_vars.json.
Undeclared Fields.Consequence: A future OPA rule can still evaluate these guidance rules by parsing the declared destination/recipient_email argument at input.args.*, so this is expressible; flagged here only because the specific domain literals are guidance-sourced constants rather than schema-declared values, which downstream phases should encode as policy constants, not as an additional undeclared runtime field.

Undeclared Fields.Declared by: Declared nowhere with integrity: system_vars.json declares a roles list (['employee','manager']) but no loader for system_vars.json was found in the inspected tree; the only runtime role value (opa_client.current_user_context['user_role'], vocabulary ['user','manager']) is self-asserted by the Streamlit client with no authentication and is not currently propagated into any OPA-visible field.
Undeclared Fields.Consequence: Every role-conditioned guidance rule is currently unenforceable at a trustworthy pre-execution point: the value exists at runtime but has no documented integrity mechanism, and its vocabulary ('user') does not match system_vars.json's declared vocabulary ('employee'), which the next phases should treat as an open reconciliation gap rather than assume is a simple renaming.

Undeclared Fields.Declared by: Declared by both view_team_compensation and export_compensation_data as select_fields (optional list[str], default null).

handoff.Summary: Analyzed examples/RagChatbot_MCPServer: 10 registered MCP tools over SSE (mcp_server.py), all with an implementation finding (no Unknowns) cross-checked against tool_definitions.json with no name/signature mismatches. Layers identified: Streamlit agent/client with LLMGuard prompt/output scanning, MCP transport/dispatch with zero pre-execution checks, tool implementations backed by static in-memory HR/compensation/purchase fixtures, a fully-built but entirely unwired OPA client/schema-transform layer (opa_client.py), and an external OPA server that is never called from any live tool path. 3 runtime-subject fields recorded, all self-asserted client-side with no authentication or integrity mechanism, and none currently reach any OPA-visible field via an active code path; system_vars.json itself was not found to be loaded by any inspected file. 31 tool-argument rows recorded across all 10 tools; several required arguments material to guidance (department and id on both compensation tools, report_data, external_sharing across two tools, amount's relation to budget limits, category/justification on purchase) are implementation-Ignored or merely Echoed rather than Acted on, meaning the described behavior in tool docstrings/guidance does not match what the code does. 4 undeclared-field gaps recorded, the most significant being that no trustworthy, declared field currently identifies requester role/team for any role-conditioned guidance rule (1,2,3,4,5,6,9,10,16), and that view_team_compensation/export_compensation_data ignore their own department/id arguments and instead always return a hardcoded manager's team. Enforcement points: the OPA-interceptable pre-execution hook at MCP tool dispatch is structurally available (all tool arguments are declared and present at that point) but currently has zero enforcement; the only active controls are prompt-layer LLMGuard scans (input allowlist can override a block; output scan skips deny-marker messages and only redacts a short hardcoded list of example literal values, not the full fixture dataset). Open gaps for Phase B: reconcile system_vars.json's declared role vocabulary/loading with the runtime code's actual (self-asserted, unauthenticated) role source; treat department/id arguments on the two compensation tools as currently non-functional for scoping; note the unresolved llm_guard_copy import and the unresolved set_user_role tool call as Unknown, not proven-missing, per the shared analysis rules.
